In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how children learn grammar.
the question of whether children's acquisition of grammar can be accounted for by frequency effects.
the role of frequency in the acquisition of grammar.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of frequency in language acquisition is not yet clear.
frequency effects are not the sole determinant of the learning of language.
frequency effects are not the only factors that influence children's acquisition of grammar.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
frequency is a factor in first language acquisition, but that it is only one of a number of factors and its importance varies depending on the type of structure under consideration.
frequency effects in first language acquisition have been shown to be real, important, and pervasive.
frequency of occurrence in the input is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for language learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that

frequency effects are important in first language acquisition and that the relationship between the relative frequencies in the input and the acquisition of grammar is a complex one that is not well-understood.
frequency effects in first language acquisition are not simply a matter of associationist learning, but that they interact with other cognitive factors in the learning process.
frequency effects are not the whole story but that they play an important role in language acquisition.
